idiom_name: container object keyed by KeyPath plus @Injected(\Container.service)
implementation_notes: Swift has no standard container, so the classic structure is hand-written: a container object holding factories or lazily built instances keyed by an explicit KeyPath, with a property wrapper such as Factory's @Injected(\.service) resolving at the point of property access and a resolve function for imperative use. Registration happens once at app start (App init or AppDelegate), lifetimes are the container's policy (singleton, per-container, transient), and the resolver stays injectable so tests can substitute a container. Constructor injection remains the default for types you construct yourself; the wrapper exists for types the platform constructs - view controllers from storyboards, App Intents, SwiftData models.
pitfalls: Lazy properties resolved through a shared container hide cycles: two services that need each other recurse until the stack overflows, and the compiler cannot see it.
@Injected resolves on first property access, so a missing or renamed key is a crash at use time; make the key path a required member of the container so the compiler catches drift.
A global shared container makes tests order-dependent - build a per-test container instance (Swinject's Container, Factory's container with a scope) instead of mutating the shared one.

variants.name: SwiftUI environment lookup
variants.idiom_name: @Environment(\.key) read from EnvironmentValues set with environment(_:_:)
variants.implementation_notes: Inside SwiftUI the framework supplies its own locator: values are installed with the environment(_:_:) modifier and read back through @Environment and an EnvironmentValues key path (or an observable object's type), which is a keyed ambient lookup scoped to the view hierarchy rather than to the process. Custom entries are declared once with the @Entry macro, so the set of resolvable values is part of the app's types and a subtree can shadow a value for its descendants. Use it for presentation-level dependencies (formatters, clocks, managers, actions) and keep domain services in injected initialisers, since non-view code cannot read the environment.
pitfalls: Reading an observable object from the environment by type throws at run time when no ancestor installed it; the key-path form with a default value is the safe shape.

The environment is a per-subtree lookup: model or service code cannot read it, so coupling non-view layers to it ends up passing values manually anyway - the same cost the pattern accepts, paid twice.
Overriding a value in a subtree changes behaviour silently for everything below it, which is powerful for previews and dangerous for app-wide services.
